title: Elimination of Uncertainty
description: Activities qualify only if intended to discover information that resolves uncertainty about a business component's capability, method or design.
summary: Elimination of uncertainty is the threshold test U.S. businesses must meet to claim federal R&D tax benefits under IRC Sections 41, 174, and 174A: activities qualify only if intended to discover information resolving uncertainty about a business component's capability, method, or appropriate design. Taxpayers need not exceed industry common knowledge, but eligibility ends once uncertainty is eliminated.

body.text: Elimination of uncertainty is the threshold test U.S. businesses must meet to claim federal R&D tax benefits under IRC Sections 41, 174, and 174A: activities qualify only if intended to discover information resolving uncertainty about a business component's capability, method, or appropriate design. Taxpayers need not exceed industry common knowledge, but eligibility ends once uncertainty is eliminated.

The Elimination of Uncertainty (EOU) criterion serves as the foundational statutory and regulatory threshold for classifying research and development (R&D) activities as eligible for current deductions or elective amortization of domestic research or experimental (R&E) expenditures under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 174A, mandatory amortization of foreign R&E expenditures under IRC Section 174, and the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under IRC Section 41. Under Treasury Regulation (26 CFR) § 1.174-2(a)(1) and § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), expenditures represent research and development costs in the "experimental or laboratory sense"—and are undertaken for the purpose of "discovering information"—only if the underlying activities are intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product or business component. Uncertainty exists under these governing regulations if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of the business component. Once technical uncertainty is resolved, subsequent commercial manufacturing, deployment, or routine quality-control activities cease to qualify under either regime.

items: Abandonment of the "Common Knowledge of Skilled Professionals" Standard (T.D. 8930 vs. T.D. 9104): Earlier commentary characterized Treasury Decision (T.D.) 8930 (published January 3, 2001, 66 FR 280, 2001-1 C.B. 433) as "proposed regulations" and suggested that qualified research must still push beyond the common knowledge base of skilled professionals in the field. In fact, T.D. 8930 was promulgated as final regulations effective January 3, 2001, and its requirement that research obtain knowledge that "exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals" was formally abandoned by the Department of the Treasury and the IRS in final regulations issued under T.D. 9104 (published and effective January 2, 2004, 69 FR 22, applicable to taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003). Current 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) expressly provides that a taxpayer is not required to seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals; rather, the legal inquiry turns strictly on whether information available to the taxpayer establishes capability, method, or appropriate design.

Enactment of IRC Section 174A Under Public Law 119-21 and Subsequent IRS Guidance in Rev. Proc. 2025-28 and Rev. Proc. 2026-32: While the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (Pub. L. 115-97, § 13206(a), 131 Stat. 2111) mandated 5-year capitalization and amortization for domestic R&E expenditures beginning after December 31, 2021, Congress restructured this regime in Public Law 119-21 (139 Stat. 72, enacted July 4, 2025), commonly known as the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). Section 70302(a) of Public Law 119-21 (139 Stat. 190) enacted 26 U.S.C. § 174A, permanently restoring immediate expensing under § 174A(a)—or elective capitalization and amortization over not less than 60 months under § 174A(c)—for domestic R&E expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Concurrently, § 70302(b) (139 Stat. 191) amended 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) to cross-reference § 174A, amended 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(1) to require a dollar-for-dollar reduction of domestic R&E deductions or capital charges by the § 41(a) credit unless a § 280C(c)(2) reduced credit is elected, and restricted 26 U.S.C. § 174 to foreign R&E expenditures (which remain subject to mandatory 15-year amortization). Following the July 31, 2025 American Institute of CPAs (AICPA) request for transition guidance, the IRS issued Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (2025-38 I.R.B. 393, released August 28, 2025; published September 15, 2025) and subsequently modified those automatic accounting-method procedures in Rev. Proc. 2026-32 (2026-39 I.R.B. 406, published September 21, 2026).

Judicial Clarification in Phoenix Design Group, Leon Max, and George: Properly construed, the decision did not reinstate an industry-wide "common knowledge" barrier; instead, the court held that performing standard engineering calculations using already available data is not an "investigative activity" under IRC § 174, that potential future design revisions or isolated subcomponent unknowns do not render an entire MEPF system uncertain under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(5), and that a linear six-stage professional design workflow without contemporaneous documentation of evaluated alternatives fails IRC § 41(d)(1)(C). These principles align with Leon Max v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-37 (addressing garment pattern adjustments and standard textile quality-control testing) and George v. Commissioner (2026, distinguishing pilot-model experimental supply trials from unsubstantiated base-period estimates).

Updated Form 6765 Section G Mandatory Effective Date and Refund Claim Perfection Extension: Under the finalized Instructions for Form 6765 (January 2025 and December 2025 revisions), Section G (Business Component Information) remained optional for all filers for tax years beginning before January 1, 2026 (covering 2024 and 2025 original returns) and is mandatory for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025 (2026 returns filed in 2027 and subsequent years), subject to exemptions for qualified small business payroll-credit filers and qualifying small filers on original returns. Additionally, via Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) Procedural Update ts-21-0126-0032 (January 2026, amending IRM 21.7.4.4.8.3.5(16)), the IRS extended through January 10, 2027, the transition window providing taxpayers 45 days to perfect deficient amended-return research credit refund claims under 26 CFR § 301.6402-2(b)(1).

body.text: Statutory and Regulatory Foundation: Defining Elimination of Uncertainty
Origin in IRC Sections 174 and 174A and the Experimental or Laboratory Sense Standard

The Elimination of Uncertainty requirement operates as the primary legal gateway separating routine commercial engineering, manufacturing, or code compliance from tax-favored research and experimentation. Historically enacted in 26 U.S.C. § 174 (Aug. 16, 1954, ch. 736, 68A Stat. 66) and interpreted in Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) (originally promulgated by T.D. 6500, 25 FR 11402, November 26, 1960, and subsequently amended by T.D. 8562, 59 FR 50160, October 3, 1994; T.D. 9381, 73 FR 8604, February 15, 2008; T.D. 9680, 79 FR 42195, July 21, 2014; and T.D. 9989, 89 FR 17606, March 11, 2024), the statutory phrase "research or experimental expenditures" denotes expenditures incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business that represent research and development costs in the "experimental or laboratory sense". The regulatory definition generally encompasses all such experimental costs incident to the development or improvement of a product, expressly including the costs of obtaining a patent, such as attorneys' fees expended in making and perfecting a patent application.

Under the fourth and fifth sentences of 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) (incorporated into the regulations by T.D. 8562 in 1994), expenditures satisfy the "experimental or laboratory sense" standard specifically on the basis of uncertainty elimination:

"Expenditures represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense if they are for activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product. Uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product or the appropriate design of the product."

Across the 1994 regulatory framework (T.D. 8562) and the 2014 final regulations (T.D. 9680, whose newly added post-production, pilot-model, and component-level rules apply to taxable years ending on or after July 21, 2014, per 26 CFR § 1.174-2(d)), Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2 establishes four operating principles that govern how uncertainty is evaluated across industrial, manufacturing, and engineering settings. First, under the sixth sentence of 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), whether expenditures qualify as research or experimental expenditures depends strictly on the nature of the activity to which the expenditures relate, rather than the nature of the product or improvement being developed or the level of technological advancement that the product or improvement represents. Consequently, R&E eligibility is neither restricted to high-technology sectors nor defeated because the underlying product is an industrial chemical, mechanical assembly, or agricultural feed formulation. Second, under the seventh sentence of 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), the ultimate technical success, commercial failure, sale, or internal use of the product is irrelevant to determining statutory eligibility.

Third, 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(3) and (a)(4) define the scope of physical and conceptual artifacts created to resolve uncertainty. Under § 1.174-2(a)(3), the term product encompasses any pilot model, process, formula, invention, technique, patent, or similar property, whether held for sale, lease, or license to external customers or developed for use by the taxpayer in its own trade or business. Under § 1.174-2(a)(4) (added by T.D. 9680), a pilot model means any representation or model of a product—explicitly including a fully functional representation or model of the product as a whole or, to the extent component-level analysis under § 1.174-2(a)(5) applies, a component of the product—that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during its development or improvement. Fourth, under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(9), R&E treatment applies only to the extent that the expenditure amount is reasonable under the circumstances (measured by what like enterprises would ordinarily pay for like activities under like circumstances, preventing disguised dividends, gifts, or loans), though the regulation expressly stipulates that this quantitative reasonableness limitation does not apply to scrutinize the "reasonableness of the type or nature of the activities themselves".

Following the enactment of Public Law 119-21 (title VII, § 70302, July 4, 2025, 139 Stat. 190–194), effective generally for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, Congress bifurcated the statutory codification of R&E expenditures along geographic lines. Domestic research or experimental expenditures are now governed by newly added 26 U.S.C. § 174A (139 Stat. 190), whereas foreign research or experimental expenditures—defined in 26 U.S.C. § 174(b) as research or experimental expenditures attributable to foreign research within the meaning of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(F)—are governed by amended 26 U.S.C. § 174 (139 Stat. 191). Both 26 U.S.C. § 174(c)(1)–(3) and 26 U.S.C. § 174A(d)(1)–(3) retain parallel statutory rules: excluding expenditures for the acquisition or improvement of land or depreciable/depletable property (while treating IRC § 167 depreciation or § 611 depletion allowances on property used in research as R&E expenditures), excluding mineral and oil-and-gas exploration expenditures, and treating any amount paid or incurred in connection with software development as a research or experimental expenditure. Under both 26 U.S.C. § 174A and 26 U.S.C. § 174, the substantive regulatory definition of "research or experimental expenditures" in 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1)—anchored in activities intended to discover information that eliminates uncertainty—remains the threshold legal test.
Integration into the IRC Section 41 Four-Part Test

While satisfying 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) brings domestic expenditures within 26 U.S.C. § 174A, qualifying for the federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities under 26 U.S.C. § 41 imposes a narrower, cumulative statutory filter. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(1)–(2), research activities related to the development or improvement of a business component constitute "qualified research" only if they are not excluded under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) or § 41(d)(4) and satisfy each element of the statutory Four-Part Test, applied separately to each discrete business component (defined in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A)–(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer):

items: The Section 174A / Section 174 Eligibility Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)): For amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, the research must be research "with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A" (as amended by Pub. L. 119-21, § 70302(b)(2)(A), 139 Stat. 191). For taxable years beginning before January 1, 2025 (unless a retroactive small-business election under Pub. L. 119-21, § 70302(f)(1) applies), IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and the unamended regulatory text of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i) reference expenditures that may be treated as expenses under IRC § 174 and 26 CFR § 1.174-2.

The Discovering Technological Information Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) & 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)–(4)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature—meaning the investigative process fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

The Business Component / Permitted Purpose Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) & § 41(d)(3)): The application of the discovered technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, undertaken for a qualified purpose relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality.

The Process of Experimentation Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) & 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)): Substantially all—defined by 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80% or more—of the research activities with respect to the business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose described in IRC § 41(d)(3).

body.text: As detailed in the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 - Qualified Research Activities (IRS ATG, page last updated July 2, 2026), the Elimination of Uncertainty requirement structurally connects the first prong of the Four-Part Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)), the second prong (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i)), and the fourth prong (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C)). Specifically, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) defines what it means for research to be "undertaken for the purpose of discovering information" in language parallel to 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1):

"For purposes of section 41(d) and this section, research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature. Research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information if it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component. Uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of the business component."

From a textual standpoint, practitioners and auditors should distinguish between verbatim regulatory language and judicial evidentiary interpretation. Although secondary tax commentary occasionally paraphrases 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) as stating that uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer, "when reviewed objectively," fails to establish capability, method, or design, the verbatim regulatory text of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) and § 1.174-2(a)(1) does not contain the phrase "when reviewed objectively". Instead, the requirement that the unavailability of design or methodological information be demonstrated on an objective factual basis—rather than resting on subjective doubt or uncorroborated assertions—reflects IRS examination policy and U.S. Tax Court precedent interpreting § 1.174-2(a)(1) and § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), including Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, and United Stationers, Inc. v. United States, 163 F.3d 440 (7th Cir. 1998).
The Three Prongs of Technical Uncertainty: Capability, Method, and Appropriate Design

Both 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) categorize qualifying technical uncertainty into three disjunctive prongs: Capability, Method (often termed Methodology), and Appropriate Design. A foundational legal rule—codified in the fourth sentence of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) and reflected in appellate precedent such as the Tenth Circuit's decision in Tax & Accounting Software—is that a taxpayer need not face all three forms of uncertainty simultaneously. Facing technical uncertainty in any one of the three prongs as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities is sufficient to establish initial technical uncertainty.

Specifically, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) provides that a taxpayer may undertake a qualifying process of experimentation "if there is no uncertainty concerning the taxpayer's capability or method of achieving the desired result so long as the appropriate design of the desired result is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities". Nevertheless, administrative guidance and case law confirm qualitatively that Appropriate Design and Method uncertainties predominate in commercial R&D claims, because taxpayers commonly know that a target engineering outcome is physically achievable while lacking the information required to establish how to execute the manufacturing process or what exact design configuration will satisfy competing functional constraints.

headers: Analytical Scope and Hypothetical Engineering Illustration

cells: Information available to the taxpayer does not establish whether the business component can be developed or improved.
"Can we physically or technically achieve this result with defined resources?"

Analytical Scope: Addresses fundamental technical feasibility when physical, thermal, biological, material, or computational limits are tested and feasibility itself is uncertain at project inception. Hypothetical Illustration: Determining whether a newly formulated ceramic-matrix composite material can physically withstand cyclical 500°F industrial thermal stresses while reducing structural frame weight by 40% and maintaining structural integrity, or whether an imaging microchip can be fabricated to the precision required to function in a vacuum.
Information available to the taxpayer does not establish how the business component should be developed or improved.
"How will we develop, manufacture, or engineer the business component to achieve the target result?"

Analytical Scope: The taxpayer knows at the outset that the target outcome is theoretically feasible (no capability uncertainty), and may know several candidate techniques, but does not know which specific engineering route, chemical synthesis pathway, fabrication process, or algorithmic technique will achieve the desired result. Hypothetical Illustration: Determining what sequence of chemical reactions, vacuum pressures, and reactor processing temperatures will consistently remove excess feedstock and yield the required purity and color specification for a new surfactant compound.
Information available to the taxpayer does not establish the appropriate design (configuration, architecture, or specification) of the business component.
"What specific configuration, dimensions, or architectural parameters are required for the component to perform as intended?"

Analytical Scope: The taxpayer knows both that the component can be built (capability) and how to build it in principle (method), but does not know the exact blueprint, geometry, material layup, or system architecture needed to satisfy functional, performance, reliability, or quality specifications. Hypothetical Illustration: Determining the exact dimensional and architectural parameters for an advanced filtration system to handle higher flow rates without structural failure, or the precise software data-caching architecture needed to prevent synchronization bottlenecks.

body.text: Regulatory Evolution: Abandonment of the TD 8930 Common Knowledge Standard in TD 9104 and the Patent Safe Harbor

Applying the Elimination of Uncertainty standard accurately requires examining the regulatory history of the IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) "discovering information" test between 2001 and 2004. Primary Treasury Decisions and current regulations establish the contrary.

First, on January 3, 2001, the Treasury Department and the IRS published T.D. 8930 in the Federal Register (66 FR 280, 2001-1 C.B. 433, RINs 1545-AV14 and 1545-A051) as final regulations—not proposed regulations—carrying a stated effective date of January 3, 2001. Under T.D. 8930, former 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i)–(ii) imposed a restrictive, industry-wide "discovery test," providing that research was undertaken for the purpose of discovering information only if it was undertaken "to obtain knowledge that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in a particular field of science or engineering". T.D. 8930 defined such common knowledge as information that should be known to skilled professionals had they performed a reasonable investigation of the existing level of information in the field prior to undertaking the research, and expressly stated that research was not undertaken for the purpose of discovering information merely because an expenditure qualified under IRC § 174.

Second, in response to immediate taxpayer and practitioner concern that T.D. 8930 imposed an unworkable industry-novelty barrier inconsistent with statutory intent, the Treasury Department and the IRS issued Notice 2001-19 (2001-10 I.R.B. 784) on January 31, 2001. Notice 2001-19 announced a comprehensive review of T.D. 8930, specified that any regulatory changes would be proposed for public comment, and stated that the provisions of T.D. 8930 (including any changes) would take effect no earlier than the date when completion of that review was announced. On December 26, 2001, Treasury and the IRS published new proposed regulations in the Federal Register removing the T.D. 8930 discovery test, followed on January 2, 2004, by final regulations in T.D. 9104 (69 FR 22, effective January 2, 2004, and applicable to taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003, with an explicit statement in the preamble that the IRS would not challenge return positions consistent with T.D. 9104 for taxable years ending before December 31, 2003).

Third, as documented in both the preamble to T.D. 9104 and the IRS ATG, T.D. 9104 abandoned the T.D. 8930 "common knowledge of skilled professionals" standard and aligned the IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) discovery requirement directly with the 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) Elimination of Uncertainty standard. Equally important, commentators responding to the December 2001 proposed regulations noted that proposed examples disqualifying activities whose capability, method, or design was "readily discernible and applicable" were highly subjective and could be misconstrued as a variant of the abandoned T.D. 8930 discovery test. In response, Treasury and the IRS modified the final regulations in T.D. 9104 to remove all references to "readily discernible and applicable," completely deleting Examples 4 and 5 of proposed § 1.41-4(a)(8) and instructing IRS examiners in the ATG that the "readily discernible and applicable" standard is no longer applicable in pending or future examinations. Codified at 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), current law provides:

"A determination that research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature does not require the taxpayer be seeking to obtain information that exceeds, expands or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the particular field of science or engineering in which the taxpayer is performing the research. In addition, a determination that research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature does not require that the taxpayer succeed in developing a new or improved business component."

Reinforcing this taxpayer-specific inquiry, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4) explicitly states that a taxpayer "may employ existing technologies and may rely on existing principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science to satisfy" the technological-in-nature requirement. Under controlling federal regulations, therefore, qualified research need only be evolutionary to the taxpayer rather than revolutionary to the broader industry. Even where candidate engineering methods are individually known in the field, uncertainty exists under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) whenever the information available to the taxpayer at the outset does not establish whether or how those methods will achieve the capability, method, or appropriate design of the taxpayer's business component. Conversely, if the information already available to the taxpayer's personnel—through existing plans, vendor specifications, standard engineering formulas, or prior in-house work—already establishes capability, method, and appropriate design without investigative experimentation, no qualifying uncertainty exists.

Finally, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) provides a regulatory Patent Safe Harbor. Under this provision, the issuance of a patent by the Patent and Trademark Office under the provisions of 35 U.S.C. § 151—other than a patent for design issued under the provisions of 35 U.S.C. § 171 (meaning a utility patent rather than a design patent)—constitutes conclusive evidence that a taxpayer has discovered information that is technological in nature and intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component. However, two explicit limits bound this safe harbor: first, issuance of such a patent is not a precondition for credit availability; and second, as the T.D. 9104 preamble confirmed in declining to expand the safe harbor, a utility patent conclusively satisfies only § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), leaving the taxpayer obligated to substantiate all remaining requirements of IRC § 41(d), including the Process of Experimentation test under § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6).
Strategic Gatekeeping: Filtering Routine Development and Mandating Experimentation
Legislative History of the Tax Reform Act of 1986

Initially enacted in 1981 as 26 U.S.C. § 44F (subsequently redesignated § 30 and then § 41), the federal research tax credit originally relied on IRC § 174 without an explicit statutory Process of Experimentation test. Early IRS examinations revealed that taxpayers were claiming credits for ordinary commercial product updates, cosmetic restyling, and routine pre-production development. Consequently, when Congress enacted the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (Pub. L. 99-514, 100 Stat. 2085), it substantially narrowed the definition of "qualified research" in IRC § 41(d) by adding the Technological in Nature, Business Component, and Process of Experimentation requirements.

Both the Senate Finance Committee Report and the House Ways and Means Committee Report accompanying the 1986 Act documented Congress's explicit gatekeeping rationale. In S. Rep. No. 99-313, at 694–695 (1986), quoted by the Seventh Circuit in United Stationers, Inc. v. United States, 163 F.3d 440 (7th Cir. 1998), the Senate Finance Committee stated:

"The committee believes that the definition has been applied too broadly in practice, and some taxpayers have claimed credit for virtually any expenses relating to product development. According to early data on the credit, the Treasury has reported, many of these taxpayers do not engage in high technology."

In parallel findings in H.R. Rep. No. 99-426, at 177–178 (1985) (quoted in T.D. 8930), the House Ways and Means Committee observed that taxpayers had applied the prior definition "too broadly," claiming the credit for "virtually any expenses relating to product development," and noted that many claimants were "in industries that do not involve high technology or its application in developing technologically new and improved products or methods of production".

In the Conference Report to the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (H.R. Conf. Rep. No. 99-841, at II-71 to II-72 (1986)), Congress linked the Technological in Nature requirement directly to resolving uncertainty through a Process of Experimentation. Specifically, the conferees explained that whether research is undertaken to discover technological information depends on whether the process of experimentation utilized in the research fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science—cautioning in footnote 3 (H.R. Conf. Rep. No. 99-841, at II-71 n.3) that "[r]esearch does not rely on the principles of computer science merely because a computer is employed". Crucially, the Conference Report defined a "process of experimentation" as "a process involving the evaluation of more than one alternative designed to achieve a result where the means of achieving that result is uncertain at the outset," encompassing structured efforts to "develop, test, and choose among viable alternatives". Applying this legislative history in United Stationers, Inc. v. United States, 163 F.3d 440, 446 (7th Cir. 1998) (affirming 982 F. Supp. 1279, 1285 (N.D. Ill.)), the federal courts held that uncertainty regarding whether a project will realize its desired business or economic benefits does not satisfy IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) when the technical means of developing the product are known at the outset.
Interdependence of Elimination of Uncertainty and the Process of Experimentation

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), the existence of technical uncertainty as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities is the mandatory starting premise for a qualifying Process of Experimentation (PoE). Absent genuine technical uncertainty concerning capability, method, or appropriate design at project inception, subsequent engineering, coding, or testing constitutes execution of known parameters rather than experimentation. Where initial technical uncertainty exists, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) and the IRS ATG require a structured, three-element evaluative process that fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science:

items: Identification of Uncertainty: Identifying the specific technical uncertainty (capability, method, or appropriate design) concerning the development or improvement of a business component that is the object of the taxpayer's research activities.

Identification of Alternatives: Identifying one or more technical alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty (noting under § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) that a process of experimentation must be an evaluative process and generally should be capable of evaluating more than one alternative).
Conduct of an Evaluative Process: Identifying and conducting a process of evaluating the alternatives—through, for example, modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error methodology.

body.text: Both the concluding sentence of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) and the IRS ATG emphasize a critical compliance limitation: merely demonstrating that uncertainty existed at the outset or that uncertainty has been eliminated is insufficient to satisfy the Process of Experimentation test. As codified verbatim in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i):

"Uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of the business component (e.g., its appropriate design) does not establish that all activities undertaken to achieve that new or improved business component constitute a process of experimentation."

Treasury and the IRS added this explicit rule in T.D. 9104 out of concern that taxpayers were giving insufficient weight to the requirement that they actively conduct an evaluative process testing technical alternatives. Presenting an unresolved design specification at project kickoff and a working product at project completion does not carry the taxpayer's burden of proof; the taxpayer must substantiate the intermediate investigative and evaluative steps undertaken to resolve that unknown.

Once qualifying experimental activities are identified, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) governs the statutory "substantially all" requirement of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C). Under § 1.41-4(a)(6), the substantially all requirement is satisfied only if 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to the discrete business component—measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis—constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose described in IRC § 41(d)(3). Practitioners must distinguish this business-component-level 80% activity rule under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) (which § 1.41-4(a)(6) directs must be calculated without regard to 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)) from the separate employee-level 80% wage rule under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2) (under which all of an individual employee's services during the tax year qualify if substantially all—80% or more—of that individual's services constitute qualified research or direct supervision/support). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), if 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to a business component constitute elements of a Process of Experimentation, the remaining 20% (or less) of research activities on that business component also satisfy the substantially all requirement, so long as those remaining activities satisfy IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) (the IRC § 174A / § 174 Elimination of Uncertainty test) and are not excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4).
The Point of Uncertainty Elimination, the Shrinking-Back Rule, and Qualified Purpose Boundaries
Beyond initiating experimentation, the Elimination of Uncertainty standard establishes the temporal cutoff, component granularity, and functional boundaries of a research claim.

Temporal Cutoff Upon Elimination of Uncertainty (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1)–(2) & IRC § 41(d)(4)(A)): Research eligibility terminates at the point technical uncertainty is eliminated. Under the eighth sentence of 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), costs may be eligible under IRC § 174 / § 174A even if paid or incurred after physical production begins, but before uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of the product is eliminated. Conversely, 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2) mandates that—except as provided in the component-level rule of § 1.174-2(a)(5)—"costs paid or incurred in the production of a product after the elimination of uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of the product are not eligible". For purposes of the IRC § 41 credit, IRC § 41(d)(4)(A) additionally excludes any research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component, while IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and (C) exclude research related to adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need and duplicating an existing business component.

Component-Level Analysis and the Shrinking-Back Rule (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(5) & 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)): Both regulatory regimes prevent isolated subcomponent unknowns from automatically qualifying an entire product, while preserving eligibility at the subcomponent level where documented. Under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(5), if the Elimination of Uncertainty requirements of § 1.174-2(a)(1) are not met at the level of an overall product, eligibility is determined at the level of the component or subcomponent. Importantly, § 1.174-2(a)(5) states: "The presence of uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of certain components of a product does not necessarily indicate the presence of uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of other components of the product or the product as a whole". Similarly, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) codifies the IRC § 41 shrinking-back rule: the Four-Part Test is applied first at the level of the discrete overall business component; if those requirements are not met at that level (for instance, because uncertainty and experimentation existed only for one subsystem rather than 80% of the overall project), they are applied to the "most significant subset of elements" of the product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention, continuing until either a qualifying subset of elements is reached or the most basic element fails. Both § 1.174-2(a)(5) and § 1.41-4(b)(2) explicitly state that these component-level rules are not themselves applied as a reason to exclude qualifying research activities or expenditures.

Qualified Purpose vs. Cosmetic Exclusions and Internal Use Software Heightened Uncertainty: Even where genuine uncertainty is resolved through experimentation, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii) require that the experimentation be undertaken for a qualified purpose—relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), research is disqualified if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. Moreover, where the business component is internal use software (IUS) (software developed primarily for internal use rather than for commercial sale, lease, license, or third-party interaction outside general and administrative functions), the Instructions for Form 6765 and legislative history note that taxpayers must also satisfy the high threshold of innovation test—including significant economic risk, where the taxpayer commits substantial resources and there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that such resources would be recovered within a reasonable period.
Practical Application: Resolving Process Uncertainty in Chemical Manufacturing
Case Study Analysis: Surfactant Color, Purity, and Vacuum Reactor Optimization

Case Study Baseline: In the underlying chemical manufacturing case study, a chemical manufacturer developed a new surfactant that it had not previously produced. At project inception, technical uncertainty existed regarding whether strict color specifications and chemical purity/activity requirements for the surfactant could be met (implicating Capability and Method uncertainty). Specifically, achieving accurate color and activity on the intermediate compound required pulling a strong vacuum on the reactor to remove excess of a feedstock compound (similar to vacuum stripping vs. inert-gas stripping in ester and sulfonate surfactant synthesis). The chemistry and engineering team confronted conflicting process constraints: if too much feedstock compound was charged or if the reactor vacuum level was insufficient, the feedstock removal step—and therefore total reactor processing time—increased substantially; conversely, if any ambient air infiltrated ("was sucked into") the batch during removal of the feedstock compound, the final product color darkened rapidly, failing specification.

Four-Part Compliance Analysis: Analyzed as an illustrative compliance scenario under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)–(5) and 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1)–(2), this surfactant process optimization demonstrates all four statutory gates:

items: Existence of Initial Technical Uncertainty (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) & § 1.174-2(a)(1)): At project inception, the information available to the chemical manufacturer did not establish the exact method or reactor process design parameters—specifically, vacuum pressure, seal configuration, feedstock ratio, and holding time—capable of removing excess feedstock without air infiltration or excessive reactor cycle time.
Technological in Nature (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4)): Resolving this process trade-off relied fundamentally on principles of chemistry and chemical engineering.

Process of Experimentation (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i)): By formulating hypotheses regarding vacuum pressure and holding times, systematically testing alternative reactor configurations, and analyzing resulting batch purity and color metrics, the team conducted an evaluative process to eliminate the uncertainty.

Point of Uncertainty Elimination (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1)–(2) & IRC § 41(d)(4)(A)): Technical uncertainty was eliminated at the exact milestone when validation trials empirically confirmed optimal, repeatable production parameters and codified them into a standard operating procedure (SOP). Up to that cutoff point, the qualified wages of chemists and engineers directly conducting, supervising, or supporting the trials, along with non-depreciable raw chemical supplies consumed in experimental pilot batches, constitute Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under IRC § 41(b) and domestic R&E expenditures under IRC § 174A. All subsequent commercial batch production costs incurred after the SOP was established are routine production costs excluded under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2) and IRC § 41(d)(4)(A).

body.text: Contemporaneous logs of a fractured prototype provide persuasive factual corroboration during an examination that the initial design was uncertain. Legally, however, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) and 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), neither ultimate success nor a documented prototype failure is required; what the regulations require is objective initial uncertainty resolved through a systematic process of evaluating technical alternatives.
Hypothetical Worked Example: Applying the Uncertainty Cutoff, 80 Percent Substantially All Rule, and Section 174A Coordination

To demonstrate the quantitative mechanics of how the Elimination of Uncertainty temporal cutoff (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1)–(2)), the 80% "substantially all" Process of Experimentation threshold (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6)), the 65% contract research limitation (IRC § 41(b)(3)(A)), the 14% Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) rate (IRC § 41(c)(4)(A)), and post-OBBBA IRC Section 174A / Section 280C(c) coordination interact in calendar tax year 2025, consider the following hypothetical worked example grounded in the surfactant process optimization scenario.
Hypothetical Facts and Assumptions (Tax Year 2025)

Assume a domestic chemical manufacturer ("ChemCorp") undertakes the Surfactant Process Business Component (IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)) during calendar tax year 2025—a taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, governed by 26 U.S.C. § 174A, amended § 41(d)(1)(A), and amended § 280C(c) under Public Law 119-21. Assume ChemCorp's average annual QREs for the three preceding taxable years (2022–2024) equal $300,000. Across calendar year 2025, ChemCorp incurs $850,000 in total project expenditures spanning three chronological phases:

items: Phase 1 — Pre-Cutoff Systematic Experimentation (January 1 – August 31, 2025): Identifying reactor process method uncertainty and conducting systematic pilot-reactor trials across alternative vacuum pressures and feedstock ratios under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i). Gross costs incurred total $480,000, consisting of $300,000 in in-house IRC § 3401(a) qualified employee wages (chemists and chemical engineers performing 70% direct experimentation, allocated via contemporaneous timesheets and below the 80% individual-employee wage threshold of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)), $80,000 in non-depreciable raw chemical feedstocks and laboratory supplies consumed in experimental pilot batches (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)), and $100,000 in gross contract research payments to an unrelated U.S. third-party testing laboratory for kinetic modeling (where ChemCorp bears economic risk and retains substantial rights).

Phase 2 — Pre-Cutoff Non-Experimental Technical Support and Patent Procurement (September 1 – September 15, 2025): Before technical uncertainty is eliminated on September 15, 2025, engineers spend time documenting final reactor safety specifications and preparing patent application data—activities that satisfy IRC § 174A / 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) and are not excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4), but do not themselves constitute elements of the evaluative Process of Experimentation. Gross costs incurred total $80,000, consisting of $60,000 in in-house employee wages and $20,000 in outside patent attorneys' fees expended in making and perfecting a utility patent application on the new surfactant process.

Phase 3 — Post-Cutoff Commercial Production and Quality Control (September 16 – December 31, 2025): On September 15, 2025, validation trials confirm repeatable surfactant color and purity, eliminating technical uncertainty. Subsequent commercial batch manufacturing and routine quality control testing total $290,000, consisting of $250,000 in commercial production wages and raw materials and $40,000 in routine quality control testing of commercial batches to verify conformance to specified parameters.

body.text: Step-by-Step Calculation Method

items: Step 1 — Apply the Elimination of Uncertainty Cutoff (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1)–(2) & (a)(6)(i)): All Phase 3 expenditures ($250,000 commercial production costs + $40,000 routine quality control testing = $290,000) were incurred after technical uncertainty was eliminated on September 15, 2025, or for ordinary quality control testing. Under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2), § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i), and IRC § 41(d)(4)(A), $0 of the $290,000 is eligible for IRC § 174A R&E expensing or IRC § 41 QRE treatment (these costs are accounted for as inventory/cost of goods sold under IRC § 263A or ordinary business expenses under general tax rules). Conversely, all Phase 1 costs ($300,000 + $80,000 + $100,000 = $480,000) and Phase 2 costs ($60,000 + $20,000 = $80,000)—including the $20,000 in utility patent application attorneys' fees expressly included under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1)—were incurred domestically prior to the elimination of uncertainty to discover information concerning the surfactant process. Thus, Gross Domestic R&E Expenditures Eligible Under IRC § 174A(a) equal $480,000 + $80,000 = $560,000.

Step 2 — Verify the 80% "Substantially All" Process of Experimentation Threshold (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6)): Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) and the IRS ATG, the "substantially all" requirement is tested by comparing the research activities that constitute elements of a Process of Experimentation (Phase 1: $480,000 of research activity costs) against total pre-cutoff research activities on the business component. Measured against § 41-potentially-eligible research activity costs ($480,000 Phase 1 + $60,000 Phase 2 wages = $540,000), dividing $480,000 by $540,000 yields 88.89% (with Phase 2 wages representing the remaining 11.11%); measured conservatively against total § 174A expenditures including the $20,000 non-QRE patent legal fees ($560,000), dividing $480,000 by $560,000 yields 85.71%. Because both figures exceed the 80% threshold, the business component satisfies 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), and the remaining balance ($60,000 of Phase 2 pre-cutoff wages) also qualifies because those activities satisfy IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) (IRC § 174A) and are not excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4). Per the IRS ATG, patent procurement expenses ($20,000 in patent attorneys' fees), while allowable under IRC § 174 / § 174A, do not qualify as QREs under IRC § 41(b).

Step 3 — Compute Total Qualified Research Expenses (IRC § 41(b)): Combining eligible QRE categories yields: qualified wages (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i)) equal $300,000 (Phase 1) + $60,000 (Phase 2 balance) = $360,000; qualified supplies (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)) equal $80,000; and contract research expenses (IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) at the 65% statutory inclusion rate) equal 65% × $100,000 = $65,000. Summing these three components produces Total 2025 QREs of $360,000 + $80,000 + $65,000 = $505,000.

Step 4 — Compute the 2025 Research Tax Credit Under the Alternative Simplified Credit Method (IRC § 41(c)(4)(A)): Under the ASC method in 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(A), the base amount equals 50% of average QREs for the three preceding taxable years (0.50 × $300,000 = $150,000), Excess QREs equal $505,000 − $150,000 = $355,000, and applying the 14% ASC rate yields a Gross IRC § 41(a) Research Credit of 0.14 × $355,000 = $49,700.

Step 5 — Coordinate the IRC § 41(a) Credit with the IRC § 174A Deduction Under Amended IRC § 280C(c)(1): Under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(1) as amended by Public Law 119-21, § 70302(b)(2)(B) (139 Stat. 191) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, if ChemCorp claims the full gross IRC § 41(a) credit of $49,700 (rather than making a timely irrevocable election on its return for a reduced credit under IRC § 280C(c)(2), which reduces the gross credit by the product of the credit and the maximum corporate tax rate under IRC § 11(b) while preserving the full deduction), ChemCorp must reduce its $560,000 domestic R&E deduction under IRC § 174A(a) by the full credit allowed, resulting in a Net Allowable IRC § 174A(a) Current Deduction of $560,000 − $49,700 = $510,300.

body.text: Judicial Scrutiny and Audit Defense: Defining the Boundaries of Uncertainty
Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2024-113)

Recent U.S. Tax Court jurisprudence has intensified scrutiny on how taxpayers substantiate both technical uncertainty (IRC § 174 / 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)) and the Process of Experimentation (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) / 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)). The pivotal decision in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, Docket No. 4759-22 (decided December 23, 2024, opinion by Judge Travis A. Greaves) illustrates why routine engineering complexity, standard design calculations, and linear project workflows fail the statutory tests when objective technical uncertainty and systematic evaluation of alternatives are not contemporaneously documented.

Case Facts and Procedural Posture: Phoenix Design Group, Inc. (PDG) is a Tennessee-based multidisciplinary professional engineering firm (taxed as a C-corporation) focusing on the design of mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) systems for hospitals, laboratories, and institutional buildings. Following an R&D credit study prepared by alliantgroup that identified 238 projects across tax years 2012–2016, the IRS disallowed the IRC § 41 research credits claimed by PDG for tax years ending December 31, 2013, through December 31, 2016. As reported in case analyses by Cherry Bekaert and Strike Tax Advisory, the claimed credits generated across 2013–2016 totaled $562,798 ($138,205 in 2013; $158,031 in 2014; $138,334 in 2015; and $128,228 in 2016), which were utilized on returns for tax years 2015 through 2019 totaling $461,741 ($55,504 in 2015; $47,811 in 2016; $219,177 in 2017; $68,147 in 2018; and $71,102 in 2019), alongside 20% accuracy-related penalties assessed under IRC § 6662 totaling $91,806 ($11,101 for 2015; $9,021 for 2016; $43,835 for 2017; $13,629 for 2018; and $14,220 for 2019).

To manage the large project population, PDG and the IRS entered into two stipulations prior to trial. Under the Trial Framework Stipulation, the parties selected a representative sample of three MEPF projects—(1) the Gerald Champion Military Psychiatric Unit, (2) Baptist Memorial Health North Mississippi Oxford (BMHNMO), and (3) the Vanderbilt University Engineering and Science Building (VUESB)—agreeing that the Court's merits rulings on the sample would establish a framework to resolve the remaining projects without being formally binding on unsampled projects. Under the Penalty Stipulation, if the Court determined that one or more of the three sampled projects involved qualified research, the IRS would concede all accuracy-related penalties across all credit years; conversely, if none qualified, PDG would be liable for the IRC § 6662 penalties. Finding no qualified research in any of the three sampled projects, the Tax Court sustained the disallowance and the 20% accuracy-related penalties.
Distinguishing Investigative Activities from Routine Calculations and Creative Iteration

In Phoenix Design Group, the Tax Court's dispositive analysis centered on PDG's failure to satisfy the IRC § 174 Elimination of Uncertainty test and the IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) Process of Experimentation test. Judge Greaves's opinion established four principles governing how technical uncertainty and experimentation are evaluated in engineering and design environments:

items: Routine Calculations on Known Data Are Not "Investigative Activities" Under IRC § 174: To satisfy the Section 174 test, a taxpayer must first demonstrate that objectively available information did not establish capability, method, or appropriate design, and second, prove that it undertook investigative activities intended to discover the unavailable information. PDG failed to identify specific technical information unavailable to its engineers at project inception and provided no evidence that investigative activities occurred prior to receiving schematic block diagrams and preliminary architectural plans. In the Gerald Champion project, PDG's mechanical engineers calculated approximate system capacities and duct sizes based on airflow parameters and historical data already provided at the start of the project, and reported those figures to the architect. Performing standard engineering calculations on already available data is not an investigative activity because the engineers already possessed the information needed to address the design question.

Potential Revisions and Isolated Subcomponent Unknowns Do Not Render an Entire Business Component Uncertain: PDG argued that design uncertainty pervaded each MEPF system as a whole because designs could potentially be revised before construction ended, because the building footprint was not yet finalized, or because final specialized equipment for a single room (such as a hybrid operating room in the BMHNMO and VUESB projects) had not yet been selected. Rejecting this contention, the Tax Court held that the possibility of downstream design revisions before construction completion does not render a system technologically uncertain at the outset. Moreover, applying 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(5), the court held that uncertainty in a single component or room does not establish uncertainty across an entire MEPF system unless the taxpayer demonstrates that the system components are so technically interrelated that the narrow unknown creates uncertainty throughout the entire business component.

A Linear Six-Stage Design Process and Code Compliance Are Not a Process of Experimentation: PDG contended that executing its standard six-stage professional design workflow (Basis of Design, Schematic Design, Design Development, Construction Document, Bidding, and Construction Administration) alongside iterative load calculations and building-code compliance established a Process of Experimentation. The Tax Court rejected this contention, holding that following a linear professional design sequence, complying with building codes, and communicating calculation outputs to architects do not mirror the scientific method or demonstrate the systematic evaluation of competing technical alternatives required by IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5).

Inability to Apply the Shrinking-Back Rule Without Subcomponent Documentation: The Tax Court recognized that when an overall MEPF business component fails the Four-Part Test, the shrinking-back rule (26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)) can narrow the analysis to a specific engineering discipline (mechanical, electrical, or plumbing) or subsystem—such as a single hospital HVAC design—though not to a chronological design phase or an individual employee's task list. However, the court could not apply the shrinking-back rule to preserve any portion of PDG's claim because PDG's generic timesheets and retrospective oral testimony failed to link employee hours to specific uncertain subcomponents or experimental evaluations.

body.text: These holdings align with both earlier and subsequent U.S. Tax Court decisions policing the boundaries of Elimination of Uncertainty across commercial industries:

items: Leon Max v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-37, Docket No. 20237-16 (filed March 29, 2021, opinion by Judge Buch): Addressing tax years 2011 and 2012 of garment company Leon Max, Inc. (LMI) (litigated by petitioner Leon Max), the Tax Court denied R&D credits claimed for a pre-production garment development process involving thread-size selection, proportioning, fabric draping, pleating, print alignment, and plus-size pattern grading. Judge Buch held that LMI faced no Section 174 uncertainties because its employees already possessed the knowledge necessary to address those routine daily adjustments; that cutting and draping fabric to evaluate fit was actual garment construction rather than scientific investigation; that design activities driven by style, taste, and seasonal design factors failed the qualified purpose test under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B); and that LMI's in-house textile tests for crocking, pilling, seam strength, fabric strength, and shrinkage following standard industry guidelines constituted excluded quality control testing under former Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3) (now § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i)) rather than research to eliminate technological uncertainty.

George v. Commissioner (U.S. Tax Court, 2026): As summarized in February and November 2026 tax practice analyses by Grant Thornton and Sensiba, the Tax Court's February 2026 memorandum opinion in George confirmed that agricultural flock and feed-formulation trials outside a conventional laboratory can satisfy Elimination of Uncertainty where experimental feed inputs function as pilot models (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4)) required to test biological variables—clarifying that supply QREs are legally independent of claiming wage QREs on a trial. Simultaneously, where the taxpayer relied on broad retroactive estimates and reconstructed records rather than contemporaneous documentation, the court disallowed unsupported claims, declined to apply the Cohan rule to estimate base-period QREs, and applied the reduced 6% credit rate under IRC § 41(c)(4)(B).

body.text: Statutory and Regulatory Exclusions: Quality Control, Efficiency Surveys, and Managerial Goals

Consistent with this case law, IRS audit guidance and Treasury Regulations restrict the Elimination of Uncertainty standard to technological unknowns concerning capability, method, or appropriate design—excluding purely financial, scheduling, or managerial unknowns. The IRS Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for all Software state explicitly that project uncertainties such as "whether or not the existing staff is adequately trained to use a technology, and/or whether the project can be completed within a given schedule and budget" do not satisfy IRC § 41(d). While manufacturing initiatives frequently pursue unit-cost or cycle-time efficiencies, those efforts qualify only if achieving process efficiency requires resolving a genuine technical uncertainty in methodology, tooling design, or engineering parameters through a scientific process of experimentation.

Furthermore, 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i)–(vii) (redesignated from former § 1.174-2(a)(3) by T.D. 9680 in 2014) explicitly excludes seven categories of expenditures from the definition of research or experimental expenditures because they do not seek to eliminate technical uncertainty in the experimental or laboratory sense:

items: Quality control testing (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) & (a)(7)): The ordinary testing or inspection of materials or products to determine whether particular units conform to specified parameters—subject to the express carve-out in § 1.174-2(a)(7) clarifying that "quality control testing does not include testing to determine if the design of the product is appropriate";
Efficiency surveys (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(ii));
Management studies (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(iii));
Consumer surveys (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(iv)) (also excluded from the credit under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D));
Advertising or promotions (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(v));
The acquisition of another's patent, model, production, or process (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(vi)); and

Research in connection with literary, historical, or similar projects (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(vii) & (a)(8)) (cross-referenced to IRC § 263A capitalization rules and mirrored by the IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) exclusion for social sciences, arts, or humanities).

body.text: Proactive Substantiation, IRC Section 174A Harmonization, and Form 6765 Compliance
Contemporaneous Documentation Standards Under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(d)

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) (promulgated in T.D. 9104 and cross-referencing the general recordkeeping requirements of IRC § 6001 and 26 CFR § 1.6001-1), a taxpayer claiming a credit under IRC § 41 "must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit".

Regulatory Precision vs. Judicial Reality: As noted in the preamble to T.D. 9104, the final regulations did not impose recordkeeping requirements beyond IRC § 6001, removing the explicit "contemporaneous" documentation mandate that had appeared in T.D. 8930—so the word "contemporaneous" does not appear verbatim in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d). Similarly, Phoenix Design Group does not establish a categorical evidentiary rule barring oral testimony. In examination and litigation practice, however, Phoenix Design Group, Leon Max, and George demonstrate that contemporaneously generated technical and time-tracking records are decisive: when taxpayers rely on retrospective summaries, broad estimates, or oral testimony that lacks corroboration in—or conflicts with—contemporaneous project records, courts routinely disallow the claimed credits for failure to substantiate initial technical uncertainty, systematic experimentation, or subcomponent cost allocation.
To substantiate Elimination of Uncertainty effectively, taxpayers should implement three operational protocols:

items: Mandatory Project-Inception Uncertainty Identification Protocol: Require project charters, initial technical specifications, or kickoff design-review minutes to document the specific Capability, Method, or Appropriate Design uncertainty before experimental work begins, explicitly stating what technical information is unavailable to the team using existing designs, vendor data, or standard engineering calculations.

Activity- and Subcomponent-Level Time and Cost Mapping to Experimental Alternatives: Configure time-tracking and general ledger cost-center systems with discrete business-component and subcomponent codes aligned with Form 6765 Section G so that employee wages, supplies, computer rental costs, and contractor invoices are linked directly to the evaluation of technical alternatives (modeling, simulation, pilot models, and iterative test runs)—preserving shrinking-back eligibility under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) and separating pre-cutoff R&D from post-cutoff production.

Training Technical Personnel in Real-Time Statutory Framing: Train engineers, scientists, and software developers to retain iterations, record hypotheses, evaluated alternatives, and test outcomes as they occur, and document the exact technical milestone or SOP sign-off date at which uncertainty was resolved.

body.text: Harmonizing IRC Section 41 and IRC Section 174A Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and Rev. Proc. 2025-28

Because 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) defines qualified research directly by reference to domestic research or experimental expenditures under 26 U.S.C. § 174A, substantiating Elimination of Uncertainty under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) governs both a taxpayer's R&E deduction/amortization posture and its research credit claim. Taxpayers must align this dual-substantiation strategy with Section 70302 of Public Law 119-21 (enacted July 4, 2025, 139 Stat. 190–194), Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (2025-38 I.R.B. 393, released August 28, 2025; published September 15, 2025), and Rev. Proc. 2026-32 (2026-39 I.R.B. 406, published September 21, 2026, modifying Rev. 2022–2024 Capitalized Domestic R&E Transition & Small Business Retroactivity

Addressed by Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (Aug. 28, 2025) as modified by Rev. Proc. 2026-32 (Sept. 21, 2026): (1) All Taxpayers (OBBBA § 70302(f)(2)): May elect via automatic method change (section 7.02 of Rev. Proc. 2025-23, cut-off basis) to deduct remaining unamortized 2022–2024 domestic SRE balances either 100% in the first post-2024 tax year (2025) or ratably over 2 tax years (2025–2026); (2) Eligible Small Businesses (OBBBA § 70302(f)(1)): Taxpayers meeting the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test (≤$31,000,000 3-year average gross receipts for 2025, not a tax shelter) could elect by July 6, 2026 (per the Rev. Proc. 2025-28 weekend/holiday rule) to apply § 174A retroactively to tax years beginning after Dec. 31, 2021 (2022–2024) via amended returns, AARs, or method changes.

IRC § 280C(c) Coordination Between Credit and Deduction
Under TCJA § 280C(c)(1), capitalized SRE amounts were reduced only to the extent the § 41(a) credit exceeded the current deduction allowed.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(1) as amended by OBBBA § 70302(b)(2)(B) (139 Stat. 191), domestic R&E expenditures taken as a deduction or charged to capital account under § 174A must be reduced dollar-for-dollar by the full § 41(a) credit allowed, unless the taxpayer makes a timely, irrevocable election on its return under § 280C(c)(2) for the reduced credit (reduced by the maximum corporate tax rate under IRC § 11(b)).

If an IRS audit challenges EOU on a project, both the IRC § 41 credit and the IRC § 174A(a) deduction (along with the § 280C(c)(1) reduction, or an irrevocable § 280C(c)(2) election made on the original return) are directly impacted.

body.text: Upfront Disclosure Mandates: Redesigned Form 6765 (Sections E and G) and Amended Return Refund Claims

Alongside internal books-and-records substantiation, the IRS has redesigned Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) from an aggregate computational schedule into a detailed upfront qualitative and business-component disclosure instrument.

Form 6765 Sections E and F: Effective beginning with Tax Year 2024 returns, Section E (Other Information, Lines 37–41) requires filers to disclose the total number of business components generating QREs during the tax year, the amount of officer wages included in wage QREs, whether the filer acquired or disposed of any major portion of a trade or business in the tax year (Line 40), and whether QREs were determined under the ASC 730 Directive (Line 41). Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary, Lines 42–48) requires filers to indicate whether they must complete Section G and reports QRE totals by category (with controlled-group members filing separate tax returns reporting only the individual member's QREs on Section F lines).

Form 6765 Section G (Business Component Information, Columns 49(a)–(f) and Columns 50–56): Under the Instructions for Form 6765 (January 2025 revision and December 2025 revision released in February 2026), Section G was optional for all filers on original returns for tax years beginning before 2026 (covering both 2024 and 2025 tax years) and is mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 (beginning with 2026 returns filed in 2027), unless the filer satisfies one of two specific exemptions:

items: Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Credit Exemption: The filer is a qualified small business under IRC § 41(h)(3) (a corporation, partnership, or other non-exempt person with gross receipts under $5,000,000 for the credit year and no gross receipts for any tax year preceding the 5-tax-year period ending with the credit year) and checks the box on Form 6765 (Line 33a) to claim a portion of its research credit (capped at $500,000 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2022, per IRC § 41(h)(4)(B)(i)) as a payroll tax credit; or

Small-Filer Exemption (Original Returns Only): The filer's total QREs determined at the controlled-group level (Line 48) are $1.5 million or less and average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years (determined under IRC § 448(c)(3) without regard to subparagraph (A)) are $50 million or less, and the research credit is reported on an original return (amended returns are ineligible for exemptions and must complete Section G on retroactive claims).

body.text: Filers required to complete Section G must follow the "80%/Top 50" business component reporting rule: itemizing business components in descending order by total QREs until capturing at least 80% of total QREs, up to a maximum of 50 business components, and reporting any remaining components on a single aggregated entry labeled "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c) (note that if "Yes" is checked on Line 41 for the ASC 730 Directive, the single "ASC 730 Directive" entry in Column 49(c) does not count toward the 50-component cap, and no additional components need be itemized if that entry equals at least 80% of Line 48 total QREs). Each itemized business component row requires entity EIN (49(a)), Principal Business Activity code (49(b)), component name or unique alphanumeric identifier matching books and records (49(c), appending "sample" and attaching Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf if statistical sampling is used), component type in 49(d) (Product, Process, or All Others), software category if applicable in 49(e) (such as internal use software vs. commercial/third-party-interacting software), amended-return indicator in 49(f), and itemized QRE amounts across Columns 50–56—allocating employee wages separately across direct research, direct supervision, and direct support, alongside supplies, computer rental/lease costs, and applicable contract research expenses.

Amended Return Refund Claim Specificity and Perfection Extension Through January 10, 2027 (Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1) & IRM 21.7.4.4.8.3.5(16)): Beginning January 10, 2022 (following IRS News Release IR-2021-203), taxpayers filing an amended return (Forms 1120X, 1040X, or amended Form 1041) that includes an IRC § 41 research credit refund claim were required to submit five items of factual information at filing to satisfy 26 CFR § 301.6402-2(b)(1). Effective for claims dated June 18, 2024, and subsequent, the IRS waived two of those items at initial filing—(1) the names of the individuals who performed each research activity, and (2) the information each individual sought to discover—though examiners may still request both during an audit. Taxpayers filing an amended-return refund claim must still provide at initial filing, signed under penalties of perjury, three mandatory items (and language that merely restates Code or Treasury Regulation requirements is insufficient):

items: Identification of all business components (as defined in IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)) to which the Section 41 research credit claim relates for that claim year;
For each business component, identification of all research activities performed, including a factual description of what the taxpayer did and how it did it; and
The total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year.

body.text: Although a November 25, 2024 IRS announcement had previously extended the refund-claim perfection transition period through January 10, 2026, the IRS issued IRM Procedural Update ts-21-0126-0032 in January 2026 (amending IRM 21.7.4.4.8.3.5(16)), extending the perfection transition window through January 10, 2027. For deficient research credit claims filed between January 10, 2022, and January 10, 2027, Accounts Management issues Letter 6426C allowing the taxpayer 45 days to respond and perfect the claim; if the taxpayer fails to respond or fails to satisfy the required criteria, Accounts Management issues Letter 6424C (No Consider)—or, in Examination with appropriate managerial/PSP and Counsel concurrence, Letter 6430 (No Consideration, Section 41 Claim)—declining to process the claim without a substantive claim disallowance.
Comprehensive Documentation Checklist for Eliminating Uncertainty

cells: Establish that information available to the taxpayer at project inception did not establish the capability, method, or appropriate design of the business component (or specific subcomponent under § 1.174-2(a)(5)), without needing to exceed industry-wide common knowledge.

Dated project charters, technical requirement specifications detailing unresolved unknowns, feasibility gap analyses, and kickoff design-review minutes explaining why existing designs, vendor data, or standard engineering calculations cannot solve the problem.

Demonstrate that the process of experimentation used to discover information fundamentally relied on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science (employing existing scientific principles is permitted).

Scientific modeling studies, finite element analysis (FEA) or computational fluid dynamics (CFD) outputs, chemical or biological lab protocols, engineering load analyses, and algorithmic architecture specifications.
3. Process of Experimentation (3 Mandatory Elements & 80% Rule)

Substantiate: (1) identification of uncertainty, (2) identification of 1+ technical alternatives to eliminate it, and (3) an evaluative process (modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error) constituting ≥80% of business-component (or shrinking-back subcomponent) research activities.

Hypothesis-driven test plans, comparative trial-and-error logs, pilot-model test records (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4)), version-control commit histories, analyses of failed prototypes or rejected design alternatives, and subcomponent-coded labor records.

Tie experimentation directly to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of a defined business component, excluding style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors (and meeting IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) technical-risk rules if IUS).

Target performance benchmark sheets, validation test protocols measuring functional metrics (thermal tolerance, purity, latency, load capacity, durability), and Form 6765 Section G component mappings.
5. Contemporaneous Timing & Point of Uncertainty Elimination Cutoff

Substantiate that uncertainty existed before claimed costs were incurred, segregate domestic (§ 174A) from foreign (§ 174) R&E, allocate wages across direct research/supervision/support for Form 6765 Section G, and halt IRC § 174A / § 41 capture once uncertainty is eliminated.

Dated project initiation and SOP sign-off records, weekly employee timesheets mapped to pre-cutoff subcomponent codes, supply consumption logs, third-party research contracts, and general ledger cost-center separation of R&D vs. post-EOU production.
